passage:
Monday. Zaid told Farida everything in the college garden, before she had asked. She sat with her arms wrapped around her knees and said, "I can't say I forgive you. I don't know what I feel." He nodded and left her alone.

Saturday. On the hostel roof, Farida's friend Nandini passed her a cup of tea. "If you say yes now, is it because you want to, or because you're scared of being alone?" Farida looked at the water tank for a long time. "Scared," she said. "Mostly." Nandini didn't say anything. She just stayed.

Three weeks later. Zaid had answered every question honestly, even the ones that shamed him, and hadn't asked her to hurry. Farida told him, "I'm not there yet. Maybe I won't be. I'm not deciding to punish you. I'm just deciding slowly."

That night she slept the whole night.

qa.q: Where did Zaid tell Farida everything?
qa.a: He told her in the college garden.

qa.q: What does Farida admit to Nandini about why she might say yes?
qa.a: She admits she is mostly scared of being alone, which shows she does not want to forgive just to escape loneliness.

qa.q: What made it easier for Farida to take her time over three weeks?
qa.a: Zaid answered every question honestly, even the shaming ones, and did not ask her to hurry, while Nandini stayed with her without pushing.

qa.q: How might Zaid feel when Farida says she may never be there?
qa.a: He may feel worried and regretful, but he can see she is not punishing him, only giving herself honest time.

grounding: Shows wondering whether trust is possible after betrayal, with forgiveness left slow and unforced, and walking away kept as an option.

passage:
Dear Vandana Didi,
You asked if I've forgiven Rohit yet. The honest answer is: I don't know, and I'm learning that's allowed.
It's been two months since I found out. He has done everything he said he would: told me the full truth, ended contact with her, started counselling, and answered every hard question without getting defensive. Some days I look at him and feel the old warmth. Other days a cold wave hits and I have to leave the room.
Last week I almost said 'I forgive you' just because I was so tired of being sad, and scared of coming home to an empty flat. I stopped myself. That wouldn't be forgiveness. That would be loneliness talking.
So I've told him I need more time, maybe months. I'm watching what he does, not what he promises. And if the trust doesn't come back, leaving is a valid choice too, not a failure.
Call me Sunday?
Sunaina

qa.q: How long has it been since Sunaina found out?
Why did Sunaina almost say 'I forgive you'?
qa.a: Sunaina felt tired of being sad and scared of the loneliness of an empty flat.

qa.q: What is Sunaina's approach to forgiveness now?
qa.a: Taking more time, watching Rohit's changed behaviour rather than promises, and accepting that leaving is also valid.

qa.q: How has Rohit responded since being found out?
qa.a: He told the full truth, cut contact, started counselling and answers hard questions without getting defensive.

grounding: A letter from a young person unsure whether to forgive a partner's betrayal, refusing forced or lonely forgiveness and giving it time.

passage: Ishita, people keep asking me why I didn't give Varun another chance. So I'll tell you properly, once. I'm Swati. When I found out he'd been cheating, he begged. Flowers, long letters, 'I'll change'. My mum said good men make mistakes. And I wanted to believe him, honestly, because the idea of starting over scared me. So I tried. For three months. But every time I asked a question, he got angry, as if I was punishing him. He kept 'forgetting' to tell me where he was. The apology didn't match what he actually did. One night I realised I was staying because I was afraid of being alone, not because I trusted him. That's not forgiveness. That's fear. So I ended it. I cried for weeks. But I don't regret it. Forgiving him in my heart, maybe one day. Staying? That was my choice to make, and walking away was valid too.

qa.q: How long did Swati try after finding out?
What did Swati realise one night?
qa.a: Swati realised the staying came from being afraid of loneliness, not from trust.

qa.q: Why was walking away a valid choice for Swati?
qa.a: Varun's behaviour didn't change, and forgiveness can't be forced; leaving was as valid as staying.

qa.q: How did Swati's mum see the situation?
qa.a: She believed good men make mistakes and hoped for forgiveness.

grounding: A spoken account of trying to forgive a cheating partner, noticing that staying was fear of loneliness without changed behaviour, and choosing to walk away.
